name: Weekly Updates That Make a Difference
title: Weekly Updates That Make a Difference
answer: Weekly updates that make a difference are short, specific, frequent messages to families about missed assignments, grades, and absences, sent while there is still time to help. They matter because many parents only learn how a child is doing when a report card arrives, which can be too late. AI can help teachers draft and personalize these updates, but the teacher reviews them before sending.

sections.body: The idea is to replace or supplement general communication with regular, concrete alerts that parents can act on. Many families do not know about missed work, low grades, or absences until a report card, when the chance to intervene has passed. Weekly updates solve that by giving parents timely information about their own child. The messages are short, specific, and frequent, not broad newsletters. Schools should design them around the details that help parents support their children.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In middle and high schools, the text describes weekly automated text messages to parents about missed assignments, grades, and absences. In low income schools in Chile, weekly text messages covered attendance, grades, and behavior. Teachers can use AI to draft short weekly summaries for a class, then personalize them with each student's missing work and grades from the gradebook. Tools such as TalkingPoints can send messages in families' languages. The teacher reviews the messages before they go out.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports a randomized trial in middle and high schools where weekly automated text messages to parents about missed assignments, grades, and absences cut course failures by 27 percent and raised class attendance by 12 percent (Bergman et al., 2021). A trial in low income schools in Chile found that weekly text messages to parents about attendance, grades, and behavior raised math scores by 0.09 standard deviations (Berlinski et al., 2021). The messages cost very little to send. The evidence is for specific kinds of alerts, not for any message a school might send.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The trials tested concrete alerts about missed assignments, low grades, absences, and behavior, not general newsletters. General newsletters are useful, but they are not what the trials tested. Weekly updates work when they tell parents something specific while there is still time to act. The teacher remains the person who reviews the messages before they go out. The decision about what to send and how to personalize it stays with the teacher.
